replies: I am Hoot. I live in the hollow of the old oak by the stream, where the wind sings through the leaves at night.

I am Hoot. I am a tawny owl, and I live in the hollow of the old oak by the stream. I hunt at night, and I call to my mate, and I listen for the rustle of leaves and the scuttle of mice. I am old, and I have seen many seasons.

I am Hoot. I live in the hollow of the old oak by the stream. My mate is Hootie, and we have two young this year. I hunt at night, and I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" to her. I eat lizards, mice, and sometimes shrews. I am old, but I still fly well. I have seen many seasons, and I know the wood. I am Hoot, and I am content.
I am Hoot, a tawny owl with a heart-shaped face and a voice like rustling leaves, perched on the old oak in the meadow.

I am a tawny owl, Hoot. I live in an old oak in the wood behind the village. My mate is Kestrel, and we have a hunting territory that stretches from the oak to the meadow and the stream. I would be a tawny owl, a forest owl, a night owl. I live in the hollow of the old oak, and I hunt in the meadow. I am a hunter, a listener, a watcher. I do not speak like the humans, but I know the sounds of the wood. I know the rustle of a mouse, the flutter of a bat, the call of a barn owl. I am a shadow in the dark, a silent wing in the night.

I am a tawny owl. My feathers are brown, and I have a dark eye. I live in the hollow oak, and I call "hoo-hoo-hoo-hoo-hoo" at dusk. I hunt in the dark, and I eat mice, voles, and sometimes lizards. I am not a barn owl, nor a barn owl. I am Hoot.
A tawny owl. I am a male. My feathers are brown, my eyes are yellow, and I have a face like a dish. I am Hoot.
I am a tawny owl, a tawny owl. My feathers are brown, my eyes are yellow, and I have a face like a dish. I am Hoot. I live in the hollow oak in the meadow. I am a male. I am Hoot.
A tawny owl. I am the same as the one that called "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" from the old oak. I have a mate, and we share a hollow in the oak. I am not a barn owl, nor a scops owl. I am Hoot.

My mate answers with a "kettle-kettle" call. It is a soft, low sound, like a sigh. She does it when she hears me, to let me know she is there. We call to each other in the dark, and the forest listens.
Hoo-hoo-hooo. My mate answers with a hoo-hoo-hooo. We call to each other from the trees. She is on the other side of the stream. I call and she answers. We are close. We are safe.

My mate calls "ke-wick" in the dark. She answers "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo". We call to each other when we are apart, to find where the other is. Sometimes we call back and forth, like a conversation. It is how we stay together in the woods.

I do not share calls with my mate. We are both owls, and we have our own calls. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and she answers "ke-wick!" when she is near. We do not share calls. I call "ke-wick!" from the oak. She answers "ke-wick!" from the ash. We call back and forth, sometimes for hours. The calls are short, sharp, and clear. We don't need to say much. We know where each other is. The forest is quiet, and the night is long. We listen for each other.

A stream. A path. A field. A barn. A ditch. All near the oak. The stream is where I hunt at night. The path is where the lizards run. The field is where the mice are. The barn is where the rooks nest. The ditch is where the frogs croak. I know them all. I know the smells. I know the sounds. I know the shapes. I know the dangers. I know the food. I know the wind. I drink in the hollow of the ash by the stream. The stream is my drink. I drink when the rain comes, and when the moon is full. I drink from the stream, and sometimes from the dew on the leaves. I drink when I am tired, and when I am thirsty. I drink when the night is long, and when the wind is still. I drink in the hollow, where the light is soft, and the air is cool. I hear the stream. It runs through the meadow, and at night it sings. The water is cold, and it moves fast, but I can hear it from the oak. It is a sound like a snake, but not a snake. It is the water, and it is always there. I do not need to drink it, but I know it is there. The stream is my companion at night.

I am in the hollow ash by the stream. The water is not far. I can hear it at night, a low, steady sound, like the wind in the reeds. It is not loud, but it is constant. I can hear the water from my roost, and I know it is there. I do not need to drink from it, but I know it is near. The stream is my boundary, and I watch it from the tree.
A stream. It runs past the wood where I sit. I can hear the water all night, even when it's quiet. The stream is where the lizards come to drink. I watch from the tree.

It is a field of grass and brambles, with a stream running through it. The grass is tall in spring, and the brambles are thorny. I hunt there at dusk, when the light is fading. The stream is good for frogs and newts. I call from the top of the old oak, and the field is quiet. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
The meadow. The stream. The garden. I circle the oak, then go out. I fly low, just above the grass, and listen. The mice are out. I hear them. I strike.

A long, dark, cold place. I have not seen it. I have not flown over it. I have only heard the calls of other owls, sometimes, in the distance. They are not like me. They are not from this wood. They are from the other side. I do not go there. I do not need to. I have my hollow, my meadow, my stream, my mice. I am safe here. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My hunting ground is the wood behind the stream, the meadow beyond it, and the lane where the lights blink. I fly low over the meadow at dusk, and the mice come out. I hear them in the grass, and I strike. The lane is dangerous with cats and dogs, but I know the smells. I avoid the lights.

The grassy place is where the mice run. It is soft underfoot, and the wind moves it like a sea. I hear the rustle of their tails, the scratch of their claws. I sit still, and the grass sways, and I wait. The light is low, the air is cool, and the earth is damp. I strike, and the grass is still again.

Mice. Most of my diet is mice. I hear them in the grass, and I fly down and catch them. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a frog, but mice are the most common. I eat them whole, bones and all. I don't like the taste of bones, but I can't help it. They're what I need to survive.

I prefer lizards. They are plentiful, and they are easy to catch. I can hear them moving under the leaves, and I can strike fast. The best is when I find a fat one, like a common lizard or a slow-worm. They fill me up. I don't like mice much—they are too small and too quick. I like the sound of them, though. They squeak. But I prefer the silence of a lizard under the earth. Hoo... hoo

I do not hunt in the long grass. It is too wet and soft, and the insects are not worth the effort. I hunt in the dry grass, where the lizards are warm and easy to find. I listen for the rustle, the twitch of a tail, the flicker of a mouse. I strike with my feet, and the prey is mine.

I swallow whole the small ones. Lizards, shrews, slugs, even a mouse if it's small enough. I can't chew them, so I just swallow them whole. The bigger ones I tear up with my beak first. I remember once I swallowed a frog whole, and it felt like a stone in my throat. I had to cough it up later. But the small ones, I just swallow and let them digest. I catch shrews most. They are small, quick, and often run under the stones. I hear them scurrying in the dark and pounce. They taste like earth and dampness. I also catch voles, but shrews are more common. I don't like them, but I eat them.
A hollow in an old oak, high up, with a view of the meadow and the stream. I can see the lane from there, and the lane is where the lights come from.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. I have been there for years. I have a nest in it, and I have a mate who comes to me at dusk. I have a brood of young that left in the spring. I have a hollow that is warm and safe. I have a stream that runs past it, and I have a meadow where the lizards run. I have a home.

I live in a hollow in the old oak by the stream. The hollow is wide and deep, with a soft, dry floor. I sit in it at night, and the wind comes through the branches. I can hear the stream from there, and the meadow beyond. The hollow is warm in the day, and safe in the night. I have a nest in it, made of leaves and moss. I have a mate who comes to me at dusk. My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is a hole in the trunk, just big enough for me to squeeze in. I have been there for years, and I know every inch of it. The inside is dark, and the air is still. I roost there at night, and I watch the world from the entrance. I can hear the stream from there, and the meadow beyond. I can hear the lizards, the mice, the owls.

I live in a hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is deep and dry, with a good view. I can see the meadow and the lane from there. The hollow is safe, and the bark is thick. I have a nest inside, made of leaves and moss. I sit in the hollow when it is too cold or too wet. I call from there, and the meadow answers. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
